title: Storage Classes: auto, static, extern, register
quickIdea: A storage class answers four questions at once: where the object lives, how long it lives, what it holds before you assign to it, and whether other files can see its name.
remember: auto is the default for a block-scope variable: stack storage, lifetime of the block, indeterminate value, no linkage. register is the same but asks for a CPU register and forbids taking its address.

static on a local changes lifetime, not scope: the object lives in the static data area for the whole program, is initialised once to zero when no initialiser is given, and keeps its value between calls.
static on a file-scope name gives internal linkage: other files cannot reach it even with extern.
extern is a declaration, not a definition: it allocates nothing and refers to the single definition elsewhere. extern int x = 5; at file scope is a definition.
A static object's initialiser must be a constant expression, so static int s = y; where y is a variable does not compile.
A static local is not part of the activation record, which is why it survives across calls and is shared by every recursion level of the same function.

example.prompt: void count(int n) { static int d = 1; printf("%d", n); printf("%d", d); d++; if (n > 1) count(n - 1); printf("%d", d); } count(3);
example.work: d is initialised once, before the first call. count(3) prints 3 and 1, d becomes 2, then calls count(2). That prints 2 and 2, d becomes 3, then calls count(1). count(1) prints 1 and 3, d becomes 4, and n > 1 is false, so it prints 4 and returns. Each return prints the current d, which is 4 by then, so count(2) prints 4 and count(3) prints 4.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.35 is this program and the answer is the nine digits above. The exam's favourite version of the same fact is a counter that should print 1 2 3 but prints 1 1 1 because the local was not declared static.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: void f(void) { int c = 0; c++; printf("%d ", c); } called three times - what is printed, and what changes if c is static?
variations.why: The shortest statement of what static does to a local, and the reason the 2016 trace ends in three 4s.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can the address of a register variable be taken?
variations.answer: No - & on a register object is a constraint violation, because the object may not have a memory address at all.
variations.why: The one examinable consequence of register being a request rather than a command.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A function declares static int s; with no initialiser and is called twice. What does s hold on the first call, and on the second?
variations.answer: 0 on the first call, and whatever the first call left on the second - the zeroing happens once, before the program starts.
variations.why: Tests that 'static means zero' is about initialisation, not about resetting on every call.

trap.what: Expecting each recursive call to get its own copy of a static local.
trap.why: A static local is one object for the whole program. Every activation of the function writes the same storage, so the value at the end of the recursion is what all the returns see.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.35 the three returns print 4, 4 and 4 rather than 2, 3 and 4, although the values printed on the way down were 1, 2 and 3.

check.question: How many times is static int d = 1; executed in a function called five times?
check.explanation: The initialisation of a static object happens before the program starts, not on each entry to the block.
